subject: chemistry
title: Halide ions
key_idea: Halide ions are reducing agents, and reducing power increases down the group. Concentrated sulfuric acid is reduced further by Br⁻ and I⁻ than by Cl⁻. Silver nitrate and ammonia identify the halides by the colour and solubility of the silver halide.

blocks.text: Halide ions can give up an electron, so they act as reducing agents. This section covers how reducing power changes and what happens with concentrated sulfuric acid.

items: Reducing power **increases** down the group: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻.
A larger ion has its outer electron further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily.

blocks.text: Solid sodium halides react with concentrated sulfuric acid. All of them first give a hydrogen halide as steamy fumes.

blocks.label: First step, for any halide
where: X: F, Cl, Br or I

items: Cl⁻ and F⁻ are not strong enough to reduce sulfuric acid. Only steamy white fumes of HCl or HF are seen.
Br⁻ reduces some H₂SO₄ to SO₂. It forms orange-brown bromine and choking SO₂ as well as HBr.
I⁻ is the strongest reducing agent. It reduces H₂SO₄ to SO₂, then to sulfur, then to hydrogen sulfide.

blocks.text: With iodide you see a black solid and purple fumes, a yellow solid, and a smell of bad eggs.

diagram.alt: A predictor. Pick a solid sodium halide to see what concentrated sulfuric acid does.

options.label: NaBr
results: Steamy fumes, orange-brown Br₂ vapour, choking SO₂

options.label: NaI
results: Steamy fumes, purple I₂ vapour, yellow solid S, smell of H₂S

items: Reducing power of the halide ions increases down the group.
Cl⁻ does not reduce H₂SO₄. Br⁻ gives SO₂. I⁻ gives SO₂, S and H₂S.

blocks.text: Halide ions are identified by precipitation with silver ions, then dissolving in ammonia. This section covers the method and the results.

items.text: Add dilute nitric acid to the test solution.
Add aqueous silver nitrate. A precipitate shows a halide.
Add dilute ammonia, then concentrated ammonia if the solid has not dissolved.

items: Nitric acid is added first to remove carbonate and hydroxide ions, which would also give a precipitate with silver ions.
Hydrochloric acid cannot be used, because it adds chloride ions. Sulfuric acid cannot be used, because Ag₂SO₄ is only sparingly soluble.
Ammonia distinguishes the halides. The solubility of the silver halides in ammonia falls from AgCl to AgI.

diagram.alt: A predictor. Pick a halide ion to see the silver nitrate and ammonia test results.

items: Acidified silver nitrate gives a precipitate with Cl⁻, Br⁻ and I⁻.
The colour and the solubility in ammonia tell the halides apart.

checks.q: Describe what is seen when concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid sodium bromide.
checks.a: Steamy fumes of HBr, orange-brown bromine vapour and a choking gas, SO₂.

checks.q: Explain why iodide ions are better reducing agents than chloride ions.
checks.a: The iodide ion is larger, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded. It is lost more easily.

checks.q: A solution gives a cream precipitate with acidified silver nitrate. State what happens when dilute and then concentrated ammonia is added, and name the ion.
checks.a: The precipitate does not dissolve in dilute ammonia but dissolves in concentrated ammonia. The ion is bromide, Br⁻.

blocks.text: This part covers the reactions of the hydrogen halides with ammonia and with water.

items: A hydrogen halide gas reacts with ammonia gas to form a white smoke of the ammonium halide: NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl.
Hydrogen halides dissolve in water to form acids: HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻.
HCl, HBr and HI are strong acids. Hydrogen fluoride is a weak acid.
The fumes seen in moist air are tiny drops of the acid.

blocks.text: This part covers the reaction with concentrated sulfuric acid as balanced equations.

items: NaCl + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl
NaBr + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HBr, then 2HBr + H₂SO₄ → Br₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O
NaI + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HI, then the reductions to I₂ with SO₂, S and H₂S as above
The trend in what H₂SO₄ is reduced to (nothing, SO₂, H₂S) shows the trend in reducing power.
